assumptions: subdomain node of library_archival_and_data_curation; scoped to research data management & curation
no observed dataset, expert judgment, or benchmark evidence supplied; all values are heuristic priors
covers the data lifecycle from planning through preservation, sharing, and governance for research data
FAIR is treated as distinct from open; sensitive data may be FAIR yet not open
nodes are concrete work units sized for one heavy reasoning session
exclusions: general library cataloging of published works (covered by sibling metadata/cataloging KBs)
bibliometrics and citation analysis of literature (sibling KBs)

competency_questions.question: What data will the project produce and what management, sharing, and preservation actions does the DMP commit to?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DMP node present with outputs and scope

competency_questions.question: Which curation lifecycle actions are scheduled, and when, across the project?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DATA_LIFECYCLE node and workflow schedule present

competency_questions.question: What data are selected for retention and what disposition/retention applies?
How does the data meet each FAIR facet, and how is FAIR distinguished from open for sensitive data?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FAIR_ASSESS node with F/A/I/R indicators and a FAIR-vs-privacy axis

competency_questions.question: What documentation and metadata make the data independently interpretable and reusable?
Can the analysis be re-executed from captured provenance and the reproducibility package?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PROVENANCE and REPRO_PACKAGE with rerun acceptance test

competency_questions.question: What is the legal basis, consent scope, and ethics approval governing sensitive data?
How is re-identification risk controlled before sensitive data are shared?
What license, rights, and embargo terms apply to each dataset?
Which repository and access tier fit the data type, FAIR, persistence, sensitivity, and policy needs?
How is the deposit packaged and validated to ingest, and how is the dataset identified and cited?
How are active data stored, backed up, and integrity-protected?
How are file formats kept usable through obsolescence and migration?
How is data/metadata quality assessed and RDM governed for compliance across the lifecycle?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: QUALITY_ASSESS and GOVERNANCE present with compliance rules

glossary.definition: a structured plan describing how research data are created, documented, stored, shared, and preserved
principles making data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable, emphasizing machine-actionability
a model of sequential and occasional actions for managing data from conceptualization to reuse
evaluating data to decide what to retain, at what retention, and what to dispose
the documented origin and processing lineage of data
a self-contained bundle of data, code, and environment enabling re-execution
removing or transforming identifiers to reduce re-identification risk
a long-lasting resolvable reference such as a DOI, ORCID, or ROR
verifiable bit-level integrity established via checksums
mediated, agreement-bound access to restricted data short of open release
a repository assessed for persistence and quality (e.g., CoreTrustSeal)
a formal citation of a dataset with PID, version, and access date

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established research data management and digital curation literature (Johnston, Curating Research Data, 2017; Rubin & Rubin, Foundations of Library and Information Science, 2020; DCC Curation Lifecycle Model; FAIR Guiding Principles, Wilkinson et al. 2016) and library/repository practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Author a data management plan specifying what data will be created, how it is documented, stored, shared, preserved, and who is responsible across the project lifecycle.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when funder policy or project scope changes the required data actions

pros.claim: a machine-actionable DMP (maDMP) seeds metadata, storage, and repository choices early
pros.example: DMP names the domain repository and license before data exist

pros.claim: funder-mandated DMPs unlock eligibility and reduce end-of-grant scramble
pros.example: NSF/Horizon Europe require a DMP at proposal

cons.claim: DMPs written once and never updated drift from real practice
cons.example: plan says Zenodo but team deposits nowhere

cons.claim: generic boilerplate DMPs add compliance cost without changing behavior
cons.example: copy-paste template with no repository named

failure_modes: no owner assigned to data actions
acceptance_tests: DMP names repository, metadata standard, license, and retention period
each data type has an assigned steward
DMP updated at each project milestone

nodes.definition: Map the project onto a curation lifecycle (e.g., DCC Curation Lifecycle Model) to schedule conceptualize, create, appraise, ingest, preserve, and reuse actions.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when project phase changes or new lifecycle actions become due

pros.claim: lifecycle framing prevents late, expensive curation by scheduling actions early
pros.example: appraisal scheduled at creation not at grant end

pros.claim: common reference model aligns stewards, IT, and researchers
pros.example: DCC model used as shared vocabulary

cons.claim: lifecycle models can be applied as ceremony without changing actual handling
cons.example: stages listed but no owner per stage

cons.claim: single deposit projects may not need full lifecycle overhead
cons.example: one-off dataset over-engineered

failure_modes: preservation deferred to end of project

nodes.definition: Appraise and select which data to keep, at what retention, applying value, reproducibility, legal, and cost criteria so not everything is preserved indefinitely.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when retention policy, legal hold, or reuse demand changes appraisal outcomes

pros.claim: selective retention controls long-term cost and discovery noise
pros.example: raw intermediates discarded, processed kept

pros.claim: documented disposition decisions defend deletions to auditors
pros.example: disposition log cites retention policy

cons.claim: deleting data is irreversible; wrong appraisal destroys reusable evidence
cons.example: unique field measurements deleted as intermediate

cons.claim: appraisal criteria are subjective and contested across stakeholders
cons.example: PI and steward disagree on value

acceptance_tests: disposition decisions are logged with criteria and approver
retention meets legal/funder minimum
reproducibility-critical data flagged keep
revisit_triggers: new reuse demand for discarded class

nodes.definition: Assess and improve data against FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) using indicators, distinguishing FAIR from open.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when FAIR indicators or community standards change required facets

pros.claim: FAIR targets machine-actionability, enabling automated discovery and reuse
pros.example: PID + rich metadata makes data findable by agents

pros.claim: FAIR separates accessibility protocol from openness, enabling reuse of sensitive data
pros.example: metadata public, access gated under FAIR-A

cons.claim: FAIR is often misread as 'must be open', blocking sensitive-data sharing
cons.example: team withholds data thinking FAIR forces openness

cons.claim: FAIR scores from different tools disagree and can be gamed
cons.example: two assessors give divergent FAIR grades

acceptance_tests: each FAIR facet has a concrete indicator checked
PID and machine-readable metadata present
accessible-but-not-open path documented for sensitive data

nodes.definition: Select and apply dataset-level metadata standards (DataCite, schema.org/Dataset, DDI, domain schemas) to describe data for discovery and citation.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when repository or domain metadata standards change required fields

pros.claim: standardized dataset metadata enables harvest and cross-repository discovery
pros.example: DataCite metadata harvested by DataCite Commons

pros.claim: domain schemas (DDI, ISA) carry reuse-critical structure
pros.example: DDI variable-level metadata supports secondary analysis

cons.claim: over-rich schemas raise cataloging cost and are unevenly filled
cons.example: optional DDI fields left blank, false richness

cons.claim: generic schemas drop domain-specific reuse detail
cons.example: schema.org/Dataset loses variable semantics

acceptance_tests: all repository-mandatory fields populated
schema matches discovery & reuse needs
metadata validates against schema

nodes.definition: Produce file-level documentation (README, data dictionary, codebook, methods) so data are interpretable and reusable independent of the creators.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when file structure, variables, or cleaning workflow changes

pros.claim: good documentation is the strongest predictor of independent reuse
pros.example: README with units lets a stranger reproduce a figure

pros.claim: codebooks disambiguate coded values and missing-data conventions
pros.example: -99 documented as missing, not a value

cons.claim: documentation written late omits tacit decisions
cons.example: cleaning steps forgotten months later

cons.claim: verbose docs without structure are hard to parse
cons.example: 20-page PDF no machine-readable dictionary

acceptance_tests: README states what/why/how/units/license
every variable defined in a dictionary
a naive reader can locate and interpret each file

nodes.definition: Capture data provenance and processing lineage (workflow steps, software versions, parameters) so transformations are auditable and reproducible.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the processing pipeline or its software environment changes

pros.claim: captured lineage lets others trace any value back to raw inputs
pros.example: PROV trace from figure to raw measurement

pros.claim: environment manifests (containers, lockfiles) enable rerun
pros.example: Dockerfile + lockfile reproduce the pipeline

cons.claim: full provenance capture is costly and often partial
cons.example: manual steps in a GUI left unlogged

cons.claim: provenance standards (PROV) are verbose and underused
cons.example: PROV-O graph nobody reads

failure_modes: no link from output to input
acceptance_tests: each derived output links to its inputs and process
software & versions recorded
a third party can re-derive a key result

nodes.definition: Package code, data, environment, and instructions into a reproducible research compendium so analyses can be re-executed and verified.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when code, data, or environment dependencies change

pros.claim: a self-contained compendium turns claims into re-executable evidence
pros.example: Binder/Docker reruns all figures from one command

pros.claim: bundling code+data+env reduces reuse friction to near zero
pros.example: reviewer reruns notebook without setup

cons.claim: packaging is effort-heavy and decays as dependencies break
cons.example: container builds break a year later

cons.claim: large data make compendia heavy and hard to host
cons.example: 100GB bundle exceeds repository limits

failure_modes: code without data or vice versa
acceptance_tests: a clean environment reproduces headline results
dependencies pinned/containerized
instructions enable one-command rerun

nodes.definition: Govern sensitive/personal data: legal basis, consent, ethics approval, and controlled handling so privacy and regulatory obligations are met.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when consent, ethics approval, or data-protection law constraints change

pros.claim: clear legal basis and consent scope define what sharing is permissible
pros.example: consent permits restricted reuse for health research

pros.claim: early governance prevents unlawful disclosure and project shutdown
pros.example: DPIA flags risk before collection

cons.claim: regulatory breach is irreversible and carries legal/reputational harm
cons.example: re-identifiable data posted openly by mistake

cons.claim: over-restriction needlessly blocks legitimate reuse
cons.example: blanket lockdown of non-sensitive fields

acceptance_tests: lawful basis documented for each data category
consent scope covers intended sharing
ethics/IRB approval on file before sharing

nodes.definition: Apply de-identification, anonymization, or pseudonymization with re-identification risk assessment so sensitive data can be shared safely.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when re-identification risk or external linkable data change disclosure risk

pros.claim: effective de-identification unlocks sharing of otherwise closed data
pros.example: k-anonymized microdata released to researchers

pros.claim: risk assessment turns disclosure control into a defensible decision
pros.example: documented residual-risk acceptance

cons.claim: residual re-identification risk can be irreversible once data are released
cons.example: linkage attack re-identifies anonymized records

cons.claim: aggressive anonymization destroys analytic utility
cons.example: DP noise makes data useless for the question

acceptance_tests: direct identifiers removed and quasi-identifiers assessed
residual re-identification risk below agreed threshold
utility-vs-risk tradeoff documented and approved

nodes.definition: Assign rights, license terms, and embargo/access conditions to data so reuse permissions are explicit and enforceable.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when rights, funder license mandates, or third-party rights change

pros.claim: an explicit license removes legal ambiguity for reusers
pros.example: CC0 lets reusers integrate data without permission

pros.claim: embargoes reconcile sharing mandates with priority/competitive needs
pros.example: 12-month embargo until publication

cons.claim: wrong or missing license blocks lawful reuse and is hard to retract
cons.example: data released CC-BY but contain third-party rights

cons.claim: over-restrictive licenses defeat sharing intent
cons.example: NC clause blocks legitimate commercial reuse

acceptance_tests: each dataset has an explicit, compatible license
third-party/IP rights cleared
embargo terms recorded and enforceable

nodes.definition: Select an appropriate repository (domain vs generalist, certified vs not) matching data type, FAIR support, persistence, and policy requirements.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when funder mandates, repository policy, or certification status change

pros.claim: domain repositories add reuse-critical metadata and community discovery
pros.example: GenBank for sequences beats a generalist

pros.claim: certified (CoreTrustSeal) repositories give persistence assurance
pros.example: CTS repository commits to succession planning

cons.claim: choosing a non-persistent repository risks future data loss and is costly to migrate
cons.example: lab website disappears, links rot

cons.claim: generalist repositories may lack domain metadata, lowering reuse
cons.example: Figshare lacks variable-level schema

acceptance_tests: repository provides persistent IDs and FAIR metadata
persistence/certification assessed
repository policy matches funder/journal requirements

nodes.definition: Prepare and execute deposit: package data and metadata to repository ingest requirements and pass submission/quality checks.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when repository ingest requirements or the data version to publish change

pros.claim: meeting ingest specs upfront avoids rejected or partial deposits
pros.example: BagIt package passes fixity at ingest

pros.claim: deposit-time checks catch missing metadata before publication
pros.example: ingest rejects record lacking required fields

cons.claim: published deposits are hard to correct, version, or retract
cons.example: wrong file version published and cited

cons.claim: access/embargo misconfiguration leaks or over-restricts data
cons.example: embargoed file set public by default

acceptance_tests: deposit passes repository ingest and fixity checks
access/embargo settings verified
correct data version confirmed before publish

nodes.definition: Mint and manage persistent identifiers (DOIs for data, ORCID, ROR, sample IDs) and keep their metadata and resolution current.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a versioning event, URL change, or metadata correction affects PID bindings

pros.claim: PIDs provide stable, citable references resilient to URL change
pros.example: DOI resolves after the repository reorganizes URLs

pros.claim: PID graphs (DOI-ORCID-ROR) enable automated attribution and impact tracking
pros.example: ORCID auto-credits the dataset author

cons.claim: a published DOI is effectively permanent; reassignment breaks the scholarly record
cons.example: DOI repointed to wrong dataset, citations corrupted

cons.claim: stale PID metadata or dead landing pages erode trust
cons.example: DOI resolves to a 404 landing page

acceptance_tests: each published dataset has a resolvable PID with a landing page
PID metadata kept current after updates
no duplicate DOIs for the same object

nodes.definition: Establish data citation practice (formal citation with PID, version, access date) and credit so datasets are cited and tracked as first-class outputs.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when data citation standards or dataset versioning change recommended citation

pros.claim: formal data citation makes datasets countable, citable outputs
pros.example: dataset cited like an article with DOI+version

pros.claim: versioned citations point to the exact data used
pros.example: citation pins v2.1 with access date

cons.claim: data citation norms are unevenly adopted across fields
cons.example: journal lists data only in acknowledgments

cons.claim: ambiguous version citation undermines reproducibility
cons.example: citation omits which version was analyzed

failure_modes: credit not attributed to data authors

nodes.definition: Provide secure active storage with backup, versioning, and access control during the project, separating working storage from preservation.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when data volume, security classification, or storage platform changes

pros.claim: robust backup prevents catastrophic active-phase data loss
pros.example: 3-2-1 backup survives a drive failure

pros.claim: versioned active storage prevents accidental overwrite loss
pros.example: snapshot recovers a clobbered file

cons.claim: active-phase data loss before deposit can be unrecoverable
cons.example: laptop stolen with only copy of fieldwork

cons.claim: conflating active storage with preservation hides format/persistence risk
cons.example: working share treated as the archive

acceptance_tests: data have tested backups (3-2-1)
access control matches sensitivity
working vs preservation storage separated

nodes.definition: Establish fixity: generate and periodically verify checksums so silent corruption (bit rot) of stored/preserved data is detected.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when storage media, replica topology, or fixity-check cadence changes

pros.claim: periodic fixity verification catches silent corruption before it propagates
pros.example: scheduled check flags a bit-flipped file

pros.claim: checksum manifests prove a deposited object is unchanged
pros.example: ingest fixity matches deposit fixity

cons.claim: undetected corruption is irreversible once all backups carry it
cons.example: corrupt file replicated to every backup

cons.claim: fixity at scale costs compute and storage for manifests
cons.example: billions of small files slow to verify

acceptance_tests: checksums exist for all preserved objects
fixity verified on a defined schedule
corruption triggers alert and recovery

nodes.definition: Manage file formats for preservation: prefer open/archival formats, monitor obsolescence, and migrate at-risk formats over time.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when format obsolescence signals or preservation policy change migration needs

pros.claim: open/archival formats reduce long-term obsolescence risk
pros.example: CSV+schema preferred over a proprietary binary

pros.claim: planned migration preserves usability as software disappears
pros.example: old format normalized before its reader dies

cons.claim: format migration can irreversibly lose data fidelity or features
cons.example: lossy migration drops embedded annotations

cons.claim: normalization to open formats can strip domain-specific structure
cons.example: instrument metadata lost on conversion

acceptance_tests: preservation copies in preferred/open formats where feasible
format obsolescence monitored against a registry
migrations validated to preserve essential properties

nodes.definition: Assess data quality and metadata completeness against criteria (completeness, validity, consistency) before and after deposit.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when quality criteria or intended reuse change fitness-for-use thresholds

pros.claim: systematic QA catches defects before they reach reusers
pros.example: schema validation flags out-of-range values

pros.claim: quality scoring prioritizes remediation effort
pros.example: worst-completeness fields fixed first

cons.claim: automated checks miss semantic/contextual errors
cons.example: valid-but-wrong coded values pass schema

cons.claim: quality criteria vary by intended reuse
cons.example: fitness depends on the secondary question

nodes.definition: Establish RDM governance: roles, institutional/funder policy compliance, audit, and review gates spanning the data lifecycle.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when institutional or funder policy, audit findings, or roles change

pros.claim: clear governance assigns accountability and enables audit
pros.example: named data owner accountable for each dataset

pros.claim: policy-compliance gates prevent non-compliant sharing/retention
pros.example: gate blocks deposit lacking ethics approval

cons.claim: heavy governance can slow research and be ignored
cons.example: approval bottleneck routed around informally

cons.claim: governance without enforcement is decorative
cons.example: policy exists but no audit ever runs

acceptance_tests: each dataset has an accountable owner
funder/institutional policy compliance checked
review gates enforced before irreversible actions

nodes.definition: Design tiered data access (open, registered, controlled/restricted) with mediation, data-use agreements, and safe-access environments so data are as open as possible, as closed as necessary.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when data sensitivity, access policy, or available secure environments change

pros.claim: tiered access enables reuse of sensitive data without open release
pros.example: controlled-access genomic data via a DAC

pros.claim: safe-haven/secure environments allow analysis without data egress
pros.example: TRE lets analysts compute without downloading

cons.claim: misconfigured access tiers can leak restricted data irreversibly
cons.example: controlled file mistakenly exposed at open tier

cons.claim: heavy mediation slows legitimate reuse and burdens requesters
cons.example: months-long DAC turnaround deters reuse

failure_modes: restricted data exposed at wrong tier
acceptance_tests: each tier maps data sensitivity to access controls
controlled access requires an enforced data-use agreement
access decisions are logged with approver

edges.why_related: the DMP sets the data actions the lifecycle schedule operationalizes
edges.benefit_of_coupling: plan drives a concrete action schedule
edges.risk_of_conflict: scheduling before planning misallocates effort
edges.example: DMP names sharing, lifecycle times appraisal/deposit
edges.resolution_rule: fix DMP scope before re-sequencing lifecycle

edges.why_related: the DMP flags sensitive data categories that trigger governance
edges.risk_of_conflict: governing before classifying data wastes effort
edges.example: DMP marks personal data, triggering DPIA
edges.resolution_rule: classify in DMP before designing controls

edges.why_related: the DMP's volume and security needs determine active storage design
edges.risk_of_conflict: storage chosen before volume estimate misfits
edges.example: DMP volume estimate sizes the storage tier
edges.resolution_rule: update storage when DMP volume changes

edges.why_related: the DMP names roles and policies the governance model enforces
edges.risk_of_conflict: governance without plan-defined roles is vague
edges.example: DMP RACI feeds the governance model
edges.resolution_rule: revise governance when DMP roles change

edges.why_related: DMP sharing intentions define the FAIR targets to assess against
edges.risk_of_conflict: assessing FAIR before sharing intent set is premature
edges.example: DMP commits to FAIR, assessment checks facets
edges.resolution_rule: re-scope FAIR when DMP sharing intent changes

edges.why_related: the lifecycle schedules appraisal as a defined action
edges.risk_of_conflict: appraising off-schedule causes rework
edges.example: lifecycle places appraisal at creation
edges.resolution_rule: re-time appraisal when lifecycle changes

edges.why_related: FAIR findability/interoperability gaps drive metadata standard choice
edges.risk_of_conflict: picking metadata before FAIR gaps known misfits
edges.example: FAIR-I gap forces an interoperable schema
edges.resolution_rule: re-select metadata when FAIR facets change

edges.why_related: dataset metadata frames the file-level documentation required
edges.risk_of_conflict: documenting before metadata model is decided drifts
edges.example: schema variables drive the data dictionary
edges.resolution_rule: update docs when metadata model changes

edges.why_related: documentation of methods is the basis for structured provenance capture
edges.risk_of_conflict: capturing provenance without method docs is unanchored
edges.example: methods narrative becomes a PROV trace
edges.resolution_rule: extend provenance when documented methods change

edges.why_related: captured lineage and environment feed the reproducible compendium
edges.risk_of_conflict: packaging without provenance can't reproduce
edges.example: environment manifest packaged for rerun
edges.resolution_rule: rebuild package when provenance/environment changes

edges.why_related: the legal basis and classification scope what must be de-identified
edges.risk_of_conflict: de-identifying before legal basis is set may over/under-mask
edges.example: DPIA scope drives quasi-identifier removal
edges.resolution_rule: redo de-id when classification/legal basis changes

edges.why_related: legal basis and consent constrain which license terms are lawful
edges.risk_of_conflict: licensing before legal basis risks unlawful terms
edges.example: consent permits only restricted reuse license
edges.resolution_rule: relicense when consent/legal basis changes

edges.why_related: sensitivity classification determines required access tiers
edges.risk_of_conflict: designing tiers before classification misroutes data
edges.example: restricted class mapped to controlled tier
edges.resolution_rule: retier on reclassification

edges.why_related: residual re-identification risk bounds how open an access tier can be
edges.benefit_of_coupling: de-id result sets the safe tier
edges.risk_of_conflict: ignoring residual risk over-opens a tier
edges.example: high residual risk forces controlled tier
edges.resolution_rule: raise tier restriction when residual risk is high

edges.why_related: license and embargo terms must be supported by the chosen repository
edges.risk_of_conflict: selecting a repo that can't honor the license forces re-deposit
edges.example: embargo support required from the repository
edges.resolution_rule: reselect repo if it cannot enforce the license

edges.why_related: FAIR support requirements (PID, metadata, persistence) constrain repository choice
edges.risk_of_conflict: choosing a non-FAIR repo undermines goals
edges.example: FAIR-F requires a PID-minting repository
edges.resolution_rule: reselect repo when FAIR requirements change

edges.why_related: appraisal of what to keep should precede committing data to a repository
edges.risk_of_conflict: depositing before appraisal wastes repository cost
edges.example: only retained data deposited
edges.resolution_rule: re-appraise before re-depositing

edges.why_related: the chosen repository's ingest spec governs deposit packaging
edges.risk_of_conflict: packaging before repo choice forces re-packaging
edges.example: BagIt spec from the selected repository
edges.resolution_rule: re-package when repository ingest spec changes

edges.why_related: metadata records must satisfy ingest's required-field checks
edges.risk_of_conflict: ingest before metadata complete is rejected
edges.example: ingest validates mandatory fields
edges.resolution_rule: fix metadata when ingest checks fail

edges.why_related: documentation is bundled into the submission package at deposit
edges.risk_of_conflict: depositing without docs lowers reuse
edges.example: README included in the submission package
edges.resolution_rule: update package when documentation changes

edges.why_related: PID metadata (DataCite) is derived from dataset metadata
edges.risk_of_conflict: minting a PID before metadata yields a thin record
edges.example: DataCite record built from dataset metadata
edges.resolution_rule: update PID metadata when dataset metadata changes

edges.why_related: a PID is assigned and bound to the landing page during deposit
edges.risk_of_conflict: publishing before PID binding breaks citation
edges.example: DOI minted and bound at publish
edges.resolution_rule: rebind PID if deposit object/version changes

edges.why_related: the PID is the anchor of the recommended data citation
edges.risk_of_conflict: citing without a PID is unstable
edges.example: citation built around the DOI + version
edges.resolution_rule: update citation when PID/version changes

edges.why_related: stored objects are the targets of checksum generation and verification
edges.risk_of_conflict: fixity without managed storage is unanchored
edges.example: checksums over the managed store
edges.resolution_rule: re-baseline fixity when storage changes

edges.why_related: fixity-verified bytes are the input to safe format migration
edges.risk_of_conflict: migrating unverified bytes risks propagating corruption
edges.example: verify fixity before migrating a format
edges.resolution_rule: re-verify fixity after any migration

edges.why_related: appraisal decides which data warrant preservation-format effort
edges.risk_of_conflict: migrating discarded data wastes effort
edges.example: only retained data normalized
edges.resolution_rule: re-scope migration on appraisal change

edges.why_related: metadata completeness is a primary input to quality assessment
edges.risk_of_conflict: assessing quality before metadata exists is partial
edges.example: QA scores metadata completeness
edges.resolution_rule: re-run QA when metadata changes

edges.why_related: documentation completeness is assessed as part of data quality
edges.risk_of_conflict: QA without docs misses interpretability defects
edges.example: QA checks README/dictionary coverage
edges.resolution_rule: re-run QA when documentation changes

edges.why_related: quality assessment should pass before deposit to avoid publishing defects
edges.risk_of_conflict: depositing before QA publishes defects
edges.example: QA sign-off precedes publish
edges.resolution_rule: re-deposit corrected data after QA fails

edges.why_related: QA defects trigger revision of documentation and dictionaries
edges.risk_of_conflict: unbounded QA-doc looping stalls
edges.example: QA flags an undocumented variable; docs updated
edges.resolution_rule: stop when QA defect list is empty

edges.why_related: QA gaps in metadata trigger metadata correction
edges.risk_of_conflict: endless QA-metadata cycling wastes effort
edges.example: QA finds a blank mandatory field; metadata fixed
edges.resolution_rule: stop when mandatory fields pass

edges.why_related: governance policy bounds permissible handling of sensitive data
edges.risk_of_conflict: handling that exceeds policy is non-compliant
edges.example: policy forbids cross-border transfer without approval
edges.resolution_rule: escalate to governance when handling exceeds policy

edges.why_related: retention policy and legal holds constrain appraisal/disposition
edges.risk_of_conflict: disposition violating policy is non-compliant
edges.example: legal hold blocks scheduled deletion
edges.resolution_rule: block deletion under a legal hold

edges.why_related: compliance gates must pass before irreversible publish/deposit
edges.risk_of_conflict: publishing without compliance is a breach
edges.example: gate blocks deposit lacking ethics approval
edges.resolution_rule: hold deposit until compliance gate passes

edges.why_related: retention-for-reuse pressure conflicts with data-minimization for privacy
edges.risk_of_conflict: keeping sensitive data longer than lawful is a breach; deleting destroys reuse
edges.example: keep raw health data vs GDPR minimization
edges.resolution_rule: minimization dominates for personal data; appraise within lawful retention

edges.why_related: FAIR-accessibility/openness pressure conflicts with privacy restriction
edges.risk_of_conflict: pushing openness can disclose personal data; over-closing defeats FAIR
edges.example: FAIR-A vs do-not-disclose personal data
edges.resolution_rule: privacy dominates; satisfy FAIR via metadata-open, data-controlled

edges.why_related: full reproducibility bundling conflicts with not exposing sensitive raw data
edges.risk_of_conflict: bundling raw sensitive data leaks it; withholding breaks rerun
edges.example: compendium needs raw data that cannot be shared
edges.resolution_rule: privacy dominates; provide synthetic/controlled-access data for rerun

edges.why_related: format migration can alter bytes, conflicting with provenance fidelity
edges.risk_of_conflict: migration without recording it breaks lineage fidelity
edges.example: normalization changes file, provenance must note it
edges.resolution_rule: record migration as a provenance event; keep original where feasible

edges.why_related: data citation and PID management both center on stable identifiers but are distinct work units
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating them hides citation-policy work
edges.example: both rely on the DOI but solve different problems
edges.resolution_rule: keep citation policy and PID minting as separate nodes

conflict_axes.trigger: sharing/openness pressure meets privacy and legal restriction on personal data
resolution_order: confirm lawful basis and consent scope
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: privacy and legal compliance dominate openness; achieve FAIR via open metadata + controlled-access data
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if no de-identification or access tier can make sharing lawful

conflict_axes.trigger: reuse-driven retention conflicts with privacy-driven data minimization
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: data minimization dominates for personal data within lawful retention; otherwise retain reuse-critical data
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if retention exceeds lawful limit or deletion destroys unique evidence
conflict_axes.example: keep raw health records vs GDPR minimization

conflict_axes.trigger: domain repositories add reuse-critical metadata but a generalist may be the only persistent option
resolution_order: check for a persistent certified domain repository
fall back to generalist with rich metadata
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: prefer a persistent domain repository; if none is trustworthy, use a certified generalist with domain metadata added
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if no domain repository is persistent/certified

conflict_axes.trigger: richer metadata/documentation improves reuse but raises curation cost and unfilled-field risk
resolution_order: budget curation effort in the DMP
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: reuse-critical fields dominate: never drop a mandated field for cost; trim only non-critical optional richness
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if curation budget cannot cover mandatory fields
conflict_axes.example: DDI variable-level detail vs cataloging effort

conflict_axes.trigger: migrating to open/current formats fights obsolescence but can lose fidelity or features
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: essential-property preservation dominates; migrate only when validated and retain the original where feasible
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if migration cannot preserve essential properties
conflict_axes.example: lossy normalization vs keeping a dying proprietary format

conflict_axes.trigger: full reproducibility wants raw data+code while disclosure rules forbid exposing sensitive raw data
resolution_order: assess what can be safely shared
provide synthetic or controlled-access data for rerun
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: disclosure rules dominate; provide controlled-access or synthetic data and open code/methods for partial reproducibility
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if no safe surrogate data exist for an external rerun
conflict_axes.example: open compendium needs unshare-able raw data

conflict_axes.trigger: pressure to deposit/publish quickly conflicts with compliance and quality gates
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: compliance and quality dominate speed; never publish past a failed ethics, license, or QA gate
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a deadline forces publishing before gates pass
conflict_axes.example: publish-now pressure vs missing ethics approval

conflict_axes.trigger: a published PID must stay stable while data corrections demand updates
resolution_order: version the dataset rather than repoint the PID
mint a new PID for the new version
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: PID stability dominates: never repoint a published DOI; issue a versioned PID and relate versions
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a correction would otherwise require repointing a published PID
conflict_axes.example: DOI repoint vs new version DOI

conflict_axes.trigger: automated curation throughput conflicts with human review of irreversible/high-risk actions
resolution_order: route high-risk/irreversible actions to human review
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: human review dominates for irreversible or high-risk actions (deletion, sensitive release, PID publish)
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if automation would finalize a high-risk action without review
conflict_axes.example: auto-publish vs DAC review for controlled data

edge_cases.trigger: team interprets FAIR as a mandate to make all data open
edge_cases.failure_mode: sensitive data disclosed or sharing wrongly abandoned
edge_cases.example: personal survey data posted openly under a FAIR push
edge_cases.detection_method: check whether any data tagged FAIR-A are personal and exposed openly

edge_cases.trigger: appraisal disposes data later found to be unique and reusable
edge_cases.failure_mode: irreversible loss of unique research evidence
edge_cases.detection_method: verify disposition log flags uniqueness and reproducibility before deletion
resolution: keep a quarantine period before purge

edge_cases.trigger: a new external dataset enables linkage re-identification of released data
edge_cases.example: anonymized records re-identified after a new registry is published
edge_cases.detection_method: re-run re-identification risk against newly available linkable datasets
resolution: raise access tier or withdraw release

edge_cases.trigger: a published DOI is repointed to a different/corrected object
edge_cases.failure_mode: scholarly record corruption; citations resolve to wrong data
edge_cases.example: DOI silently repointed to v2 breaking v1 citations
edge_cases.detection_method: diff PID target before/after; alert on any change to a published PID
resolution: mint a new versioned PID instead

edge_cases.trigger: corruption replicated to all backups before fixity detection
edge_cases.failure_mode: no clean copy remains; corruption is permanent
edge_cases.example: bit-flip replicated to every backup before any check ran
edge_cases.detection_method: compare current checksums to baseline manifest across replicas

edge_cases.trigger: format migration silently drops essential properties
edge_cases.example: embedded instrument metadata lost on conversion
edge_cases.detection_method: validate migrated copy against defined essential properties and the original

edge_cases.trigger: the wrong data version is deposited and published
edge_cases.failure_mode: incorrect data cited; correction is costly post-publication
edge_cases.example: draft file published instead of the QA-passed final
edge_cases.detection_method: confirm version hash against the QA-approved release before publish

edge_cases.trigger: data deposited without a license or with third-party-rights conflict
edge_cases.failure_mode: lawful reuse blocked or rights infringed
edge_cases.example: data released CC-BY containing licensed third-party imagery
edge_cases.detection_method: check each deposit has a compatible license and cleared third-party rights

edge_cases.trigger: data deposited without a usable README or data dictionary
edge_cases.failure_mode: data are findable but uninterpretable, blocking reuse
edge_cases.example: CSV with cryptic headers and undocumented missing-value codes
edge_cases.detection_method: run a reuse check: can a naive reader interpret each file and variable

edge_cases.example: endless metadata-QA cycling over trivial fields
edge_cases.detection_method: track QA defect count and iteration count against thresholds
resolution: accept residual low-risk defects with a record

edge_cases.trigger: computed scores or labels drift from formulas/evidence after edits
edge_cases.example: edited a base metric but left final_importance stale
edge_cases.detection_method: recompute all derived fields with the formula script and diff against stored values
resolution: fix labels to heuristic where no data exist

workflow.objective: fix data scope, lifecycle actions, roles, and governance before any technical choice
acceptance_tests: DMP names repository, metadata standard, license, retention
each data type has a steward
workflow.do_first_because: the DMP, lifecycle, and governance are the highest-coupling foundations all later steps depend on

workflow.objective: classify sensitivity, establish legal basis/consent, and set retention/appraisal before sharing decisions
acceptance_tests: lawful basis documented per category
retention meets legal/funder minimum
workflow.do_first_because: legal basis and classification are high-irreversibility constraints that gate all sharing and disposition

workflow.objective: assess FAIR, choose metadata standards, and produce documentation for interpretability
acceptance_tests: each FAIR facet has an indicator
mandatory metadata fields populated
README interpretable by a naive reader
workflow.do_first_because: metadata and documentation are high-coupling foundations for deposit, PID, and quality

workflow.objective: capture provenance and assemble a reproducibility package
acceptance_tests: each output links to inputs and process
a clean environment reproduces headline results
workflow.do_first_because: reproducibility depends on documentation and feeds quality and deposit

workflow.objective: apply de-identification, assign licenses, and design access tiers for lawful sharing
acceptance_tests: residual re-identification risk below threshold
each dataset has a compatible license
tiers map sensitivity to controls
workflow.do_first_because: disclosure controls are high-risk, high-irreversibility steps that must pass before any sharing

workflow.objective: select a trustworthy repository matching data type, FAIR, persistence, license, and policy
acceptance_tests: repository provides PIDs and FAIR metadata
persistence/certification assessed
policy matches funder/journal
workflow.do_first_because: repository choice is high-irreversibility and gates deposit packaging and PID

workflow.objective: assess data and metadata quality and remediate defects before deposit
acceptance_tests: mandatory fields valid
no high-severity defects open
documentation completeness verified
exit_criteria: QA passed or residual low-risk defects recorded
workflow.do_first_because: QA must pass before publish to avoid distributing defects and forcing post-publication correction

workflow.objective: package and deposit data, mint PIDs, configure access, and establish citation
acceptance_tests: deposit passes ingest and fixity
access/embargo verified
resolvable PID with landing page
workflow.do_first_because: deposit and PID publication are irreversible and require all upstream gates to pass first

workflow.objective: establish active storage/backup, fixity, and preservation-format management
acceptance_tests: tested 3-2-1 backup exists
checksums exist and verified on schedule
preservation copies in preferred formats where feasible
workflow.do_first_because: preservation underpins integrity for deposit and long-term reuse and can run alongside QA/deposit

workflow.objective: run compliance audit, human review of high-risk/irreversible actions, then lock artifacts and update the DMP
acceptance_tests: policy compliance verified
every high-risk node human-reviewed
validation rerun passed
workflow.do_first_because: hard lock is only permitted after dependency, validation, and human-review gates all pass

dominance_rules.trigger: a sharing/openness action would disclose personal or restricted data
dominance_rules.rule: never open data past a lawful-basis/consent boundary; satisfy FAIR via open metadata + controlled-access data
dominance_rules.required_action: block open release until de-identification or an access tier makes sharing lawful
dominance_rules.example: FAIR-A push blocked because data are identifiable personal records

dominance_rules.trigger: a faster path skips a gate and risks correctness, compliance, or integrity
dominance_rules.rule: never accept a speed win that fails a compliance, QA, license, or fixity gate
dominance_rules.required_action: hold deposit/publish until the failed gate passes
dominance_rules.example: deadline-driven publish rejected for missing ethics approval

dominance_rules.trigger: an irreversible or high-risk action (deletion, sensitive release, PID publish) is queued
dominance_rules.rule: irreversible/high-risk actions require human review before execution
dominance_rules.required_action: route the action to a reviewer and record the decision
dominance_rules.example: automated purge of unique data blocked pending review

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-value node is unblocked-looking but an upstream prerequisite is unmet
dominance_rules.rule: respect dependency precedence over raw importance when sequencing
dominance_rules.required_action: schedule the prerequisite first; keep the dependent in draft
dominance_rules.example: deposit deferred until repository selection and QA complete

dominance_rules.trigger: quality or validation has not passed but a lock is requested
dominance_rules.rule: no soft/hard lock before QA and validation pass
dominance_rules.required_action: block lock until QUALITY_ASSESS and validation rerun pass
dominance_rules.example: record set lock refused until mandatory fields validate

dominance_rules.trigger: a correction tempts repointing a published PID
dominance_rules.rule: never repoint a published PID; version instead
dominance_rules.required_action: mint a new versioned PID and link versions
dominance_rules.example: DOI repoint replaced by a new v2 DOI

dominance_rules.trigger: a numeric estimate implies more certainty than the evidence supports
dominance_rules.rule: evidence labels and grounding dominate apparent numeric precision; keep heuristic labels without data
dominance_rules.required_action: label estimates heuristic and avoid observed/experimental claims
dominance_rules.example: no observed labels used because no dataset was supplied

dominance_rules.trigger: an assertion lacks a resolvable source reference
dominance_rules.rule: every claim must resolve to a source; unsupported claims are downgraded or removed
dominance_rules.required_action: attach SRC_HEURISTIC_PRIOR or remove the claim
dominance_rules.example: edge weight tied to SRC_HEURISTIC_PRIOR rather than an invented source

dominance_rules.trigger: a convenient dependency edge would create a cycle
dominance_rules.rule: preserve dependency acyclicity; convert the weaker link to sequence/feedback
dominance_rules.required_action: demote the weaker edge to sequence or feedback and record the repair
dominance_rules.example: QA->metadata made a feedback edge to avoid a cycle

dominance_rules.trigger: new objects are added without traceability links
dominance_rules.rule: traceability from source to question to node to workflow dominates raw object count
dominance_rules.required_action: link each new object to a CQ, source, and workflow step before lock
dominance_rules.example: a new node without a CQ ref is rejected until linked

anti_rework_rules.rule: resolve the DMP, lifecycle, and governance before technical data actions
anti_rework_rules.rationale: actions taken without a plan misallocate effort and force redo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: data deposited before any DMP exists
anti_rework_rules.example: repository chosen before the DMP named requirements

anti_rework_rules.rule: classify sensitivity and establish legal basis before any sharing decision
anti_rework_rules.rationale: sharing before classification risks unlawful, irreversible disclosure
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: license assigned before legal basis known
anti_rework_rules.example: data released before consent scope was checked

anti_rework_rules.rule: assess FAIR gaps before selecting metadata standards and repository
anti_rework_rules.rationale: choosing schema/repo before FAIR gaps forces re-selection
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: metadata schema picked before FAIR-I gap known
anti_rework_rules.example: generalist repo chosen, then FAIR-F requires a PID minter

anti_rework_rules.rule: finalize dataset metadata before minting persistent identifiers
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a PID minted on thin metadata yields a poor, hard-to-fix record
anti_rework_rules.example: DataCite record thin because metadata was incomplete at minting

anti_rework_rules.rule: pass quality assessment before deposit and publication
blocked_until: QA passed or residual low-risk defects recorded
anti_rework_rules.rationale: publishing defects forces costly post-publication correction
anti_rework_rules.example: draft file published instead of the QA-passed final

anti_rework_rules.rule: select the repository before packaging the deposit
anti_rework_rules.rationale: packaging to the wrong spec forces re-packaging
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: BagIt package built before repo choice
anti_rework_rules.example: submission re-bagged after a different repository was selected

anti_rework_rules.rule: verify fixity before any format migration
anti_rework_rules.rationale: migrating unverified bytes can propagate corruption irreversibly
anti_rework_rules.example: migration ran on an already-corrupt source file

anti_rework_rules.rule: complete human review and validation rerun before hard lock
anti_rework_rules.rationale: hard-locking before review forces full change-control to undo
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: hard lock requested before review sign-off
anti_rework_rules.example: PID publication locked before the disclosure review passed

anti_rework_rules.rule: record an appraisal decision before any disposition or deletion
anti_rework_rules.rationale: deletion is irreversible; undocumented disposal destroys reusable evidence
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: data deleted with no disposition record
anti_rework_rules.example: unique measurements purged with no logged appraisal

iteration_protocol.trigger: validator or QA report flags a failure
acceptance_tests: every failure mapped to a subsystem

iteration_protocol.trigger: multiple defects compete for repair effort
iteration_protocol.detection: rank by risk x irreversibility x detectability
acceptance_tests: highest-risk defects scheduled first
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: queue ordered and no high-risk defect unscheduled

iteration_protocol.trigger: a fix touches a high-coupling or locked node
acceptance_tests: all dependents identified

iteration_protocol.trigger: a defect is assigned for repair
iteration_protocol.detection: map failure type to repair owner via repair_routing
acceptance_tests: fix applied by the correct owner

iteration_protocol.detection: re-run the formula script over the KB
acceptance_tests: all computed scores within tolerance 0.02

iteration_protocol.trigger: repairs were applied to a locked or high-coupling component
acceptance_tests: overall_status is pass or pass_with_warnings
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: validation passes with no new failures

iteration_protocol.trigger: an update_signal condition fires for a node
acceptance_tests: posterior change >= delta recorded
iteration_protocol.stop_condition: no node exceeds the revisit delta

iteration_protocol.trigger: risk>=0.80, confidence<0.65, or an irreversible action is queued
acceptance_tests: every high-risk/irreversible item has a sign-off

human_review_required_for: hard lock of any dataset or record set

checks.expected: dependencies and conflicts on distinct edges
every node references a CQ; all refs resolve

version_increment_rules: increment on any hard-locked artifact change
increment when formulas or metric weights change
lock_downgrade_rules: downgrade dependents when an upstream node changes
downgrade when an evidence label is revised
